svg.font-family: ui-sans-serif, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Partial screen updates: only changed tiles are sent
svg.desc: The renderer diffs each new frame against the one the device already holds, in 12 by 12 pixel tiles. Only the tiles that differ are sent over TCP, merged into wider blits where they are horizontally adjacent, and the device paints them onto its existing framebuffer.
svg.text: Only what changed goes over the wire
Each frame is compared with the one the device already holds, tile by tile. 20 of 400 tiles differ here — 5.0% of a full repaint.
1 — RENDERED ON THE PC
Diffed against frame N−1 in 12×12 tiles.
Filled cells differ; outlines are the 5 blits
they merge into, row by row.
diff
2 — SENT OVER TCP :6789
Nothing else is transmitted. The black here is
not sent as black — it is simply absent from
the payload.
blit
3 — PAINTED BY THE DEVICE
A whole screen was already there. The tiles
land on top of it — outlined here, invisible
in life. No full-screen repaint, no tearing.
THE ARITHMETIC
one tile
RGB565, 2 bytes a pixel
this frame — 20 tiles, 5.0%
a full 20 × 20 repaint
Wi-Fi on an ESP8266 could not
carry the full frame at 10 fps.
An ordinary frame: the numbers have not moved, only the mascot has, so the cost of the update is the size of the mascot. A frame that also carries
a new reading — a taller bar, a new axis label, a redrawn projection — touches about four times as many tiles, and is still a fraction of a repaint.
A few extra tiles ride along each frame in raster order, so a patch dropped during the initial burst is healed within one sweep rather than waiting for that region to change again.
Figure generated by docs/make_figures.py from two real consecutive frames — the tile pattern and every number above are measurements.
